name: Puliyodarai (Tamarind Rice)
cuisine: Tamil Nadu (Iyengar / temple "kovil" style; the same dish is puliyogare in Karnataka and pulihora in Andhra; sold in Mumbai at Matunga, Chembur and Sion South Indian eateries)

ingredients.name: Tamarind (imli / puli), seedless block
ingredients.householdMeasure: a lump the size of a small gooseberry (about 1 tbsp packed)

ingredients.name: Sesame oil, cold-pressed (gingelly oil / nalla ennai / til oil)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 tbsp (2 tsp for the tempering, 1 tsp for the rice)

ingredients.name: Chana dal (Bengal gram dal / kadalai paruppu), for the powder
Dry red chilli (sukhi lal mirch), for the powder
Chana dal (Bengal gram dal), for the tempering
Urad dal (split black gram, white / ulundu)
Dry red chilli (sukhi lal mirch), for the tempering

equipment: Pressure cooker (2–3 litre) for the rice
Small heavy pan or tawa for dry-roasting the spice powder
Small kadai or tadka pan for the tempering and pulikachal
Small mixer-grinder jar (chutney jar) for the powder
Small bowl for soaking tamarind and a tea strainer
Wide plate for cooling the rice
Spatula or flat spoon; measuring spoons (a normal teaspoon is fine)

steps.title: Soak the tamarind
steps.text: Put 10 g tamarind in a small bowl and pour over 100 ml hot water.
steps.visualCue: Tamarind softens and the water turns brown
steps.videoShot: Hot water poured over a dark tamarind lump.

steps.title: Rinse the rice
steps.text: Rinse 65 g (⅓ cup) rice 2–3 times until the water is nearly clear.
steps.visualCue: Water only slightly cloudy
steps.cameraCheck: The rinsed rice in the cooker

steps.title: Cook the rice
steps.text: Add 160 ml water, close the cooker and cook on medium for 3 whistles; let the pressure drop on its own.
steps.tip: Slightly firm, separate grains make the best tamarind rice; mushy rice turns pasty when mixed.
steps.visualCue: Grains fully soft but separate, no water left
steps.cameraCheck: The open cooker showing cooked rice

steps.title: Heat the roasting pan
steps.text: Put the small heavy pan on low-medium heat, dry (no oil).
steps.visualCue: A drop of water sizzles off
steps.cameraCheck: The empty pan on the flame
steps.videoShot: Water drop skittering on the pan.

steps.title: Roast the dal and coriander
steps.text: Add 2 g (½ tsp) chana dal and 2 g (1 tsp) coriander seeds and stir.
steps.visualCue: Dal turns light golden; coriander smells toasty
steps.videoShot: Spatula stirring seeds in a dry pan.

steps.title: Add chilli, fenugreek and pepper
steps.text: Add 1 dry red chilli, a pinch (0.3 g) fenugreek and 4–5 peppercorns; stir.
steps.tip: Burnt fenugreek makes the whole dish bitter; take the pan off as soon as it darkens.
steps.visualCue: Chilli puffs and darkens slightly; fenugreek turns a shade darker (not black)
steps.cameraCheck: The pan with all the spices

steps.title: Add the sesame last
steps.text: Add 3 g (1 tsp) white sesame, stir until it crackles, then tip everything onto a plate to cool.
steps.visualCue: Sesame starts popping and turns pale golden
steps.cameraCheck: The roasted spices cooling on a plate
steps.videoShot: Sesame seeds jumping in the pan.

steps.title: Grind the powder
steps.text: Grind the cooled spices to a fine powder.
steps.visualCue: Fine, sandy brown-red powder with a nutty smell
steps.cameraCheck: The powder in the jar (about 1 tbsp)
steps.videoShot: Jar opened to show the powder.

steps.title: Extract the tamarind
steps.text: Squeeze the soaked tamarind with your fingers and strain the juice into the bowl, pressing the pulp; discard the fibres.
steps.visualCue: Thick, smooth brown juice, about 90 ml

steps.title: Spread the rice to cool
steps.text: Spread the cooked rice on a wide plate, drizzle 1 tsp (4 g) sesame oil and sprinkle half the salt (0.75 g); fluff gently with a fork.
steps.visualCue: Grains glossy and separate
steps.cameraCheck: The rice spread on the plate
steps.videoShot: Oil drizzled over rice and fluffed.

steps.title: Heat the tempering oil
steps.text: Heat 2 tsp (8 g) sesame oil in the kadai on medium.
steps.visualCue: Oil shimmers; a mustard seed dropped in sizzles at once

steps.title: Splutter the mustard
steps.text: Add ¼ tsp (1 g) mustard seeds.
steps.visualCue: Seeds pop and crackle

steps.title: Fry the peanuts
steps.text: Add 10 g (1 tbsp) peanuts and fry on low-medium, stirring.
steps.visualCue: Peanuts turn golden with brown spots; skins crack

steps.title: Fry the dals
steps.text: Add 3 g (1 tsp) chana dal and 2 g (½ tsp) urad dal and stir.
steps.visualCue: Both dals turn golden-brown

steps.title: Add chilli, curry leaves, hing and turmeric
steps.text: Add the broken red chilli, 8–10 curry leaves, a small pinch (0.1 g) hing and a pinch (0.3 g) turmeric.
steps.tip: Stand back; curry leaves spit when they hit hot oil.
steps.visualCue: Curry leaves crackle and turn crisp; oil turns yellow

steps.title: Pour in the tamarind
steps.text: Add the strained tamarind juice (about 90 ml) and stir.
steps.visualCue: Loud sizzle, then a brown liquid
steps.videoShot: Tamarind poured into the hot tempering.

steps.title: Season the pulikachal
steps.text: Add the remaining salt (0.75 g) and 3 g (½ tsp) jaggery; stir.
steps.visualCue: Jaggery dissolves

steps.title: Reduce the pulikachal
steps.text: Simmer on low-medium, stirring now and then, until thick.
steps.visualCue: Thick, glossy, jam-like paste; oil separates and shows at the edges; raw tamarind smell gone
steps.cameraCheck: The thick paste with oil at the edges
steps.videoShot: Spatula drawn through the paste leaving a trail.

steps.title: Add half the spice powder
steps.text: Stir in half the ground powder (about 3 g) and cook.
steps.visualCue: Paste darkens slightly and smells nutty
steps.cameraCheck: The paste with powder mixed in

steps.title: Mix with the rice
steps.text: Tip the pulikachal over the cooled rice, add the rest of the spice powder and mix gently with a flat spoon or your fingers.
steps.tip: Fold, do not mash; broken grains go pasty.
steps.visualCue: Every grain coated an even reddish-brown, peanuts spread through

steps.title: Taste and adjust
steps.text: Taste; add a pinch of salt or a little more powder only if needed.
steps.visualCue: Sour, spicy and slightly sweet, nutty finish

steps.title: Rest before eating
steps.text: Cover and rest the rice so the flavours soak in.
steps.tip: Puliyodarai tastes better after a rest, which is why it is a classic travel and packed-lunch food.
steps.visualCue: Rice darker and more aromatic
steps.videoShot: Lid lifted to show the rested rice.

reasons: no frying, mostly unsaturated fat from sesame oil and peanuts, no cholesterol, only about 3 g added sugar, and some protein and minerals from peanuts, dals and sesame. But it is mainly white rice (about 69 g carbs, low fibre at about 4.5 g), has no vegetables, and the salt (1.5 g) is about 30% of the daily limit in one plate. Restaurant and temple versions usually use more oil and bigger rice portions, and sometimes groundnut or refined oil instead of sesame (est.).

researchRating.basis: puliyodarai is one of South India's best-loved rice dishes and a famous temple prasadam (Wikipedia, Karnataka Tourism), covered by almost every major Indian recipe site; Hebbar's Kitchen's temple-style puliyodharai shows 5/5 from about 199–239 votes across snapshots, Tarla Dalal's tamarind rice 5/5 from 7 reviews, and Mumbai food guides single out the tamarind rice at Hotel Ramashraya, Matunga (Curly Tales) and the temple puliyogare at KTR (Time Out Mumbai). Small deduction because it is seen as everyday or travel food rather than a treat, it is hard to find on Mumbai delivery apps, and vote counts outside Hebbar's Kitchen are small.

storage: Finished puliyodarai: room temperature for up to about 6–8 hours (the tamarind and oil help, but cooked rice should not sit out longer); fridge in a closed box for up to 2 days. Freezing works but the rice turns slightly crumbly. Reheat with a sprinkle of water, covered, in a pan or microwave for 1–2 minutes until steaming. Pulikachal paste alone: about 2 weeks in the fridge in a clean, dry jar, kept under a film of oil (Jeyashri's Kitchen; some sources say longer).
leftoverRemix: Puliyodarai paniyaram or stuffed paratha. Mash leftover puliyodarai with a little rice flour or besan and water, and pan-cook small patties in a paniyaram pan or on a tawa until crisp; or use it as a tangy filling in a wheat paratha. (Not Jain-specific; check the flour for gluten-free needs.)
burnOff: about 7 km of running (490 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 9.8 km of brisk walking (about 2 h at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: rice (a grain), chana and urad dal and table salt are avoided in the common North and West Indian vrat rule set (assumption: that rule set; in South Indian homes puliyodarai is cooked as a Navratri festival offering, which is not a fast).

ekadashi.reason: rice and other grains and pulses are avoided on Ekadashi in the most common rule set.

jain.reason: no onion, garlic or root vegetables (dried turmeric powder and hing only); as with all Jain meals, eat it before sunset if that rule is followed.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; keeps well unrefrigerated for some hours and is filling for sehri, though about 600 mg sodium and the tang may make some people thirsty.

jain.reason: no onion, garlic, potato, ginger or fresh turmeric root; only dried spices, dals, peanuts, tamarind and rice. Turmeric is used as dried powder (not fresh root); a strict household that avoids even turmeric powder can leave out the pinch.

vegan.reason: cooked in sesame oil; no ghee, curd, milk or honey (jaggery is plant-based).

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, so it fits a pescatarian diet.

sattvik.reason: temple-style puliyodarai is made without onion or garlic (it is a prasadam dish; Jeyashri's Kitchen tags its kovil version no-onion-no-garlic).

glutenFree.reason: no wheat in the recipe, but the pinch of hing is usually compounded with wheat flour in India; use gluten-free hing or skip it.

dairyFree.reason: no milk, curd, ghee or butter.
